newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU'S VAN MIERT BLOCKS RENAULT SPAIN SUBSIDY.
newsitem.headline: EU'S VAN MIERT BLOCKS RENAULT SPAIN SUBSIDY.

text.p: European Commissioner Karel Van Miert, in charge of competition matters, is blocking Spanish government subsidies for a Renault plant in Spain over Renault's decision to close a profitable Belgian assembly plant, he told BRTN radio on Thursday.
Van Miert told the station he would block the government aid until Renault management changed its attitude on the closure of the plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels.
Under Renault plans the Valladolid, Spain, plant had been due to take over part of Vilvoorde production.
BRTN said 500 million Belgian francs was at stake.

Van Miert told the station on Thursday morning he received the Renault dossier on Spanish government aid for additional investment in Valladolid on Wednesday. "I will block this dossier as long as Renault behaves the way it does."
He said Renault was trying to move part of a profitable operation to another location in the European Union with government aid.

"It is of course absurd that they close a profitable company such as (Renault Industrie Belgique in) Vilvoorde and carry out additional investment in Spain with government aid," he said, according to a BRTN transcript.
Last Thursday Renault unexpectedly announced it would close its Vilvoorde plant in July with a loss of 3,100 jobs.

The surprise decision sparked angry reactions from unions and the Belgian and French governments, in particular over the harsh tone of the announcement and Renault's apparent total disregard of the social consequences.

The Belgian government is suing Renault over its flouting of Belgian and European rules on informing and consulting staff on key strategic decisions. The European Commission disapproved of Renault's actions, but could do little else.
Van Miert said the dossier could be blocked for months.
"It is clear that in the current context and (given) Renault's attitude that government aid cannot be granted or... allowed when it is for purposes as is now the case," he said.
Asked whether the blocking could be seen as Commission punishment for Renault, Van Miert said, "no."

"But it is undefensible that profitable activities are moved from one side of the European Union with government aid...it can't be that with Spanish government aid (Renault) tries to lure activities away which are normally profitable."
